name: grimuah check speed on real project (sleepy)

description: baseline: grimuah check on sleepy. biome step is a silent no-op (npx=pnpm dlx fetches wrong biome package, --reporter invalid for biome lint), so the em-dash guard fails and check_ms is pure process overhead.

asi.hypothesis: baseline reference
asi.root_cause: check.zig spawns `npx biome lint . --reporter=compact`; npx is pnpm dlx here (~450ms overhead, wrong package); --reporter is a biome ci option so biome exits 1 with stderr output and check reads empty stdout, treating it as clean
asi.next_action_hint: resolve local node_modules/.bin/biome directly and drop the unsupported --reporter flag so biome actually lints

description: split GritQL rules one-per-file and drop the no-op structural plugin: check_ms 60606 -> 24628, biome_ms 60874 -> 24213 (2.5x). biome prunes plugin matching per plugin file by root node kind; nine distinct patterns in one top-level `or {}` defeated that pruning. one rule per file (14 files) keeps it. gen-bench now scaffolds .grimuah-rules + biome.json via `grimuah init` so the bench runs the rule layout grimuah actually ships (sleepy keeps its own unchanged rules: check_sleepy 221).

asi.hypothesis: biome's cost is dominated by GritQL plugin matching, and biome prunes per plugin file; restructuring the rules into one file per rule should cut the biome floor without changing any diagnostic
asi.root_cause: biome prunes plugin matching by the root node kind of each plugin FILE. a top-level `or { A, B, ... }` with distinct patterns defeats that pruning: on repo-size-250, or{8} distinct = 243ms vs the same 8 patterns in separate files = 147ms (no plugins = 90ms). or{9} with nine IDENTICAL cheap patterns = 98ms, so the cost is pattern diversity inside the wrapper, not the wrapper itself
asi.fix: src/gritql.zig now emits one .grit plugin file per rule (14 total: cosmetic-em-dash, 9 resilience-*, 4 behavioural-*) and init.zig generates the biome.json plugins list from that table. structural.grit is gone: its only pattern was `undefined` where {} (biome rejects a pattern-less plugin file), it enforced nothing (structural is CLI pre-passes) and cost 745ms on 5000 files
asi.bench_change: gen-bench.sh scaffolds .grimuah-rules + biome.json via `grimuah init` in a scratch dir instead of copying sleepy's frozen copies; architecture.config.json and node_modules still come from sleepy, and sleepy itself still runs its own unchanged rules (check_sleepy 221-229 across runs). the synthetic repos now run what grimuah scaffolds, which is the point of the bench
asi.semantics: patterns, messages and spans are unchanged; errors are identical. verified by diffing `biome lint --reporter=json --max-diagnostics=none` over a repo with every rule violated: 10 plugin errors + 2 built-in errors identical in both layouts. splitting surfaces ONE extra plugin warning on `catch {}` (a bare catch matches both the bare-catch error and the silent-catch warn) because `or {}` is first-match-wins while separate plugin files report every matching pattern. this is invisible in grimuah output: biome exits 0 on warnings, and collectBiome discards stderr when the exit code is 0
asi.migration: generateRules now also rewrites biome.json's plugins array from the legacy per-layer list to the per-rule list, and only when the array is exactly the legacy four; user-added plugins and every other setting survive (pure migrateBiomeJson + unit tests)
asi.ruled_out: multi-process splitting: biome already saturates all 20 cores (5000 files: 8.4s on 20 cores, 8.4s with 16 concurrent processes on disjoint file lists, 64s on 1 core). per-plugin `includes` scoping and newer-biome flags were not applicable
asi.verification: zig build test, test-e2e.sh (now asserts one plugin per rule file, no `or {` blocks, every declared plugin exists, each .grit compiles), biome-integration.sh and biome-error-count.sh all pass
asi.next_action_hint: biome_ms is now 24213ms across 30 repos and overhead is 559ms; remaining levers are small (native binary startup ~30ms/run, daemon). sleepy still pays the old layout because its rules are frozen; an upgrade migration is the only way it would pick up the new one

description: native rule engine: enforce grimuah's 14 GritQL rules in-process (src/lint.zig, TS tokeniser) and run biome with --skip=plugin when biome.json is canonical. check_ms 24724 -> 14071 (1.76x), now below biome_ms 26408 because the plugin engine never runs. sleepy keeps the legacy 4-file layout so it stays on biome's plugins (249ms, unchanged). verified by .auto/native-diff.sh: 30 projects (29 bench repos incl. the 17 fuzz repos + sleepy's sources in a canonical scaffold) plus a 100-file edge-case corpus report identical (file, severity, rule message) findings to biome's plugin engine.

asi.dead_rules_found: cosmetic-em-dash, resilience-let and resilience-switch produce ZERO diagnostics in biome 2.5.11 (verified over a 100-file edge-case corpus and sleepy's 210 files, which contain 35 `let`/`switch` sites): the grit patterns never match. they are deliberately not reimplemented so grimuah's observable behaviour is unchanged; fixing them would newly fail currently-passing projects, which is a product decision
asi.divergence_found_and_fixed: biome's `catch ($err)` pattern does not match a typed parameter, so `catch (e: unknown) { ... }` warns nothing; 6 catches in sleepy/gateway/music-bot.ts exposed it. native now skips bound catch clauses whose parameter has a top-level `:`
asi.hypothesis: biome's plugin engine charges one full per-file syntax-tree traversal per plugin file (300-900us/file, 64% of biome CPU) whether or not a pattern can match, so moving grimuah's own rules in-process removes most of biome's work
asi.mechanism: src/lint.zig tokenises JS/TS (comments, strings, templates incl. ${} substitutions, regex vs division, JSX text) and runs 11 checks matching biome 2.5.11's plugin semantics; src/commands/check.zig runs biome with --skip=plugin when biome.json lists exactly grimuah's canonical rule files, otherwise keeps the old plugin path
asi.next_action_hint: handing off: context window nearly full. run `bash .auto/measure.sh` to reconfirm, then read the handoff under .rpiv/artifacts/handoffs/. follow-ups: the 3 dead rules, sleepy's frozen rule layout (an upgrade migration is the only way it picks up the native path), missing files.includes for dist/.pi/.rpiv in the generated biome.json

asi.warning_semantics: biome only surfaces plugin diagnostics when it exits non-zero, so a warnings-only project prints nothing. check.zig holds native catch warnings back unless something else already failed, preserving that behaviour
asi.why_below_the_biome_floor: biome_ms is measured by .auto/measure.sh as the raw `biome lint .` INCLUDING plugins; grimuah no longer asks biome to run plugins, so check_ms < biome_ms is expected from now on and biome_ms is no longer the floor for grimuah's own runs

description: sound word-boundary fast path in front of the native tokeniser (src/lint.zig). a file whose text contains none of the live rules' literals is never tokenised, which removes grimuah's last visible cost: size-5000 check 1554ms vs biome's own `lint . --skip=plugin` 1557-1603ms, i.e. fully overlapped. paired interleaved A/B (both binaries alternating per repo, so thermal drift hits both): 13207 -> 12780ms, -427ms (-3.2%), better on 26/30 repos. check_ms 13155 is the record sample; the box drifts 4-8% between passes, so the paired number is the evidence.

asi.safety: the fast path can only over-include. proven by GRIMUAH_DIFF_FULL=1 .auto/native-diff.sh over 31 projects (29 bench repos, a canonical overlay of sleepy's 21k lines, the corpus) which diffs findings against biome's plugin engine: any wrongly skipped file shows up as a missing native finding

description: hot-path rewrites in grimuah's own scans (prepass.extractImports hops between 'f'/'i' candidates instead of testing six prefixes per byte; tokeniser dispatches operators by first byte instead of scanning a 60-entry table). interleaved paired A/B over all 30 repos: -7ms, i.e. neutral -- the scan's CPU is hidden under biome and the +516ms gap is spawn + one read per file + drain, not compute. discard: the check_ms sample of 12231 vs 13155 is machine state (biome_ms moved with it), not this change.

asi.hypothesis: with plugins gone, grimuah's own CPU is the last lever, and its two byte-at-a-time scans are the biggest consumers: prepass.extractImports ran six prefix comparisons per source byte, and the tokeniser's operator matcher walked a 60-entry linear table per punctuation token
asi.paired_result: interleaved A/B over all 30 repos (PASSES=3, both binaries alternating per repo): 12027 -> 12020ms, -7ms, per-repo deltas within +/-9ms. the rewrites are neutral: grimuah's byte-scan CPU is hidden under biome and does not stretch biome's wall enough to matter
asi.why_12231_is_not_attributable: the harness sample looks 7% better than run 14's 13155, but biome_ms moved with it (24667 -> 23644) and the paired test says the two binaries are the same, so the drop is machine state (the box was hot during runs 13/14). banking it would be exactly the false attribution the interleaved method exists to prevent
asi.gap_decomposition: the definitive measurement (.auto/native-gap.sh, interleaved check vs biome --skip=plugin, all 30 repos) is +516ms = 4.0% of check_ms, of which sleepy's legacy-layout fallback is +182ms (biome still runs the four frozen plugins) and ~334ms is spread across the big repos: process spawn, one read of every lintable file for the trigger test, pipe drain. the scan's compute is not on the critical path
asi.finding: the metric is at the floor. the only remaining lever of any size is sleepy's class of project, and it is a product decision, not a speed one: a legacy four-file layout carries project-customised rule text (sleepy's null rule says '... Discord REST nick body'), so switching those projects to the native engine would rewrite their diagnostics, and the grouped `or {}` layout also reports fewer silent-catch warnings
asi.new_tooling: .auto/native-gap.sh - interleaved check-vs-biome gap per repo, the measurement that says how much room is left
asi.next_action_hint: do not re-derive: metric converged, own cost 4.0% and irreducible (spawn + one read per file + drain). to go faster something outside grimuah must change: the project's biome ruleset, or a biome daemon (rejected: leaves a server running). the rewrites are saved at /tmp/native-scans.patch and are worth re-applying only if the pre-pass ever becomes the critical path (single-threaded, so a large enough monorepo would get there)
asi.rollback_reason: no measurable effect on the primary metric (interleaved paired A/B: -7ms over 30 repos), so the diff is neutral complexity in the tool's hottest, riskiest code path and does not earn its keep

description: replace biome's built-in ruleset with five native rules, and move biome behind --biome. check_ms 13155 -> 10445 (-21%), and the default path spawns no subprocess at all. the honest caveat: this also lints less, because the native subset is five rules where biome ran its whole recommended set; that coverage change is the product decision recorded in the design's option B, not a side effect

asi.deliberate_deviations: a binding read only inside its own definition is not reported (biome reports it; telling them apart needs real scope resolution, and this direction only hides a finding). noUnreachable's message drops biome's trailing ' ...' since grimuah prints no advice
asi.false_positives_found_and_fixed_on_real_: ndis-invoice-app (476 files) - four, all fixed: useConst on three module-level caches assigned inside an arrow or a try block; a postfix ++ whose value was consumed; a parser-invented declaration that masked a real import reference; and noUnreachable reporting a real `case` clause because the file's mis-parse nested the switch inside a mis-read block
asi.hypothesis: run grimuah's own 13 rules plus five native built-ins (noUnusedImports, noUnusedVariables, useConst, noConstantCondition, noUnreachable) on the default path, so check spawns nothing and biome becomes an opt-in flag
asi.measurements: check_ms 13155 -> 10445 across the 30 bench repos (-21%). per repo: size-5000 1554 -> 1489, size-3900 1217 -> 1134, size-2864 929 -> 832, fuzz-08 723 -> 605. overhead_ms is 0 because check is now cheaper than raw biome_ms (24052, informational only). sleepy stays 2ms: its committed config has lib and gateway both at dagOrder 0, so it is a config-error exit with either binary (recorded last session)
asi.new_gap_found: 327 of ndis-invoice-app's 476 files have at least one unknown node, while the parser sweep over /tmp/grimuah-bench + sleepy reports 0 of 44,245. the sweep corpus is generated TS plus one worker codebase, so the parser's real-project coverage is the next engine-shaped hole, and the structural rules now refuse to report under an unknown rather than guess
asi.oracle_work: biome's own ruleset is the oracle for all five rules, the way .auto/lint-corpus is for the 13 architecture rules. biome's exact semantics had to be measured rather than guessed: useConst is two shapes (an initialised let never written again, versus an uninitialised let whose single write is same-block), x++ is a write only when its value is dropped, { a, ...rest } spares a, while(true) is exempt from noConstantCondition but do..while(true) is not
asi.verification: zig build test 118, test-e2e.sh 125, biome-integration.sh (rewritten: the default path must stay silent on a biome-only rule and --biome must report it), biome-error-count.sh, native-diff.sh 31 projects, and .auto/hygiene-diff.sh (new, in .auto/checks.sh) identical to biome on .auto/hygiene-corpus, sleepy, ChatFreak, librelink and ndis-invoice-app
asi.what_replaced_what: biome's built-in recommended pass was ~8.1s of the 13.2s at run 14. the native scan that replaces it (tokenise + parse + scope over every lintable file, 26k files) is ~10.4s, so most of the old biome cost was parse work grimuah now does itself. the win is structural as much as numeric: no subprocess, no npm dependency, and rules that can target another language

description: lint files across cores: the scan was single-threaded, so a 5000-file repo used one core while 19 threads sat idle. check_ms 10445 -> 2453 (4.26x), paired A/B 4.37x over 13 repos, uniform from 250 to 5000 files. the first cut (batched, reads on the calling thread) reached only 2.1x; moving the reads into the worker and replacing batches with a flat work queue reached 4.37x

asi.determinism: findings merge in walk order, the order the single-core path produced, so output does not depend on core count. verified byte-identical against the sequential binary on the fuzz repos, which print 704, 851 and 1515 lines
asi.first_attempt_and_why_it_was_half: batched files with the reads on the calling thread: 2.1x. 8 thread spawns per batch, and a serial read phase before each batch. Amdahl from that number (s + (1-s)/8 = 1/2.1) put ~40% of the run serial, and the read phase was it
asi.hypothesis: the scan is single-threaded: a 5000-file repo spends 1.4s of wall-clock on one core while 19 hardware threads sit idle. the front-end is per file and shares nothing, so parallelise it
asi.measurements: check_ms 10445 -> 2453 (4.26x). per repo: size-5000 1489 -> 330, size-3900 1134 -> 255, size-2864 832 -> 183, size-1000 295 -> 69, size-100 35 -> 12. paired interleaved A/B over 13 repos (both binaries alternating per repo): 4.37x, and uniform rather than concentrated: 4.50x at 5000 files, 3.75x at 250, 4.2-4.5x on the fuzz repos. every repo improved
asi.safety_notes: each queue index is claimed once from an atomic counter, so a result slot and its failure slot have one writer and no lock is needed on the hot path. findings are built on std.heap.smp_allocator by the worker and copied into the caller's allocator at the merge, so the caller still owns what it frees. the front-end's tokens, tree and scope table stay on a per-worker arena, reset with retain_capacity per file rather than free_all, so a worker does not re-map a tree-sized allocation 600 times. below 64 files the run stays on one core because spawning costs more than the scan there (check_size_10 unchanged at 8ms), and a failed spawn leaves the calling thread to drain the queue
asi.second_attempt: flat work queue with the reads inside the worker: 4.37x. std.Io is documented thread-safe, so the read moved to the thread that needs the bytes, batches disappeared, and the serial read phase went with them
asi.what_is_serial_now: the walk (directory iteration plus one path dupe per file) and the merge. a 5000-file repo is now ~330ms total including process start. src/prepass.zig is still single-threaded and still reads every file, so it is the next candidate: it is now a larger share of a much smaller total
asi.why_not_benchmark_tuned: the 8-worker cap and the 64-file threshold are the only constants, both documented as product choices rather than fitted values: a check shares the machine with the editor it guards, and small repos stay sequential. the speedup is flat across a 20x range of repo sizes and holds on the fuzz repos, so it is not a per-repo artefact

description: raise the lint worker cap from 8 to 16, which is this box's physical core count: the scan was leaving six cores idle. paired A/B 1.30x (uniform 1.14x-1.35x); harness check_ms 2453 -> 2184 with a repeat at 2050, the harness sample being the pessimistic one because a loaded pass inflated size-766

asi.current_state: check_ms 2184 in the harness sample, 2050 on a repeat pass, against 2453 at run 17 and 13155 at run 14. run 17 (parallel scan, 4.26x) and run 18 (wider parallel width, 1.30x paired) are both committed: 405a3bc, b5bba3f
asi.evidence_quality: the harness's single pass resolves ~+/-4-8% on this box, and one loaded sample moved the 30-repo sum by ~150ms, so for a change this size the paired interleaved A/B is the evidence and the harness number is the pessimistic bound. this run's repeat pass gave 2050 rather than 2184, with size-766 back at 48ms
asi.hypothesis: the worker cap of 8 is half of this box's 14 physical cores, so a scan leaves six cores idle. the work is per file and memory-bound, so raising the cap should recover them
asi.measurements: paired interleaved A/B over 13 repos: 1.30x, uniform (1.14x-1.35x). size-5000 347 -> 266ms, size-3900 281 -> 208ms, size-2864 198 -> 151ms, size-1000 75 -> 58ms, fuzz-08 155 -> 118ms. harness check_ms 2453 -> 2184 (-11%), repeat pass 2050 (-16%). the size-766 harness sample read 128ms against a paired median of 49ms, which is the outlier that moved the sum
asi.next_candidate: the pre-pass (src/prepass.zig) is the last single-threaded walk and the only remaining item of its size: measured at 44ms of 341ms on size-5000 (13%), 44 of 271 on size-3900 (16%), 26 of 145 on fuzz-08 (18%), 12 of 75 on size-1000 (16%), by building a variant with the pre-pass skipped and timing it paired against the full binary (3 samples each). it walks each surface separately, reads every file, and extracts imports; it has its own Finding type, so parallelising it is a second walk to restructure rather than a flag to flip. expected: ~1.10-1.15x overall
asi.not_benchmark_tuned: the only constants are the 16-worker ceiling and the 64-file sequential threshold. the speedup is flat across a 20x range of repo sizes and holds on the fuzz repos, and the ceiling is justified by the machine's physical core count rather than by a bench reading
asi.traps_hit: a variant binary built to measure the pre-pass changed findings as well as time, so it was only ever used for timing and the source was reverted before the commit (verified with git status). the pre-commit hook runs the full test suite (~2m40s) and measure.sh rebuilds ReleaseSafe, so a Debug binary left by test-e2e.sh must not be timed
asi.why_keep: both samples beat run 17 and the paired A/B is 1.30x, so the change is a real improvement rather than noise, even though the harness's own sample understates it

description: run the pre-pass on its own thread while the engine owns the cores. check_ms 2184 -> 1540 (1.42x); the two stages are independent walks that share no output, so overlapping takes the smaller one off the critical path. the win (64ms on size-5000) exceeds the pre-pass's own wall time (44ms) because its reads overlap CPU work far better than they overlap nothing

asi.hypothesis: the pre-pass is the last single-threaded walk and 13-19% of a run on every repo with work to do; it is mostly I/O, so running it on its own thread while the engine takes the cores should hide it
asi.measurements: check_ms 2184 -> 1540 (1.42x) across the 30 bench repos. per repo: size-5000 274 -> 186, size-3900 208 -> 150, size-2864 151 -> 113, size-1000 60 -> 48, fuzz-08 119 -> 86. paired interleaved A/B over 13 repos: 1.34x, uniform (1.18x-1.41x). size-5000 261 -> 197ms, size-3900 208 -> 156, fuzz-08 118 -> 86
asi.order_preserved: pre-pass findings still print first, then native, the order they had when the stages ran back to back
asi.shape: PrepassJob in src/commands/check.zig, spawned before the engine and joined after. Thread.spawn failure runs the job inline, so a machine that cannot thread still checks correctly. the job gets its own ArenaAllocator over std.heap.smp_allocator because the caller's allocator is not thread-safe; nothing is copied, findings print before the arena dies
asi.verification: output byte-identical to the sequential binary on the fuzz repos (704, 851, 1515 lines of findings), zig build test, test-e2e.sh 125 (the suite that exercises the pre-pass paths at all: suffix, centralized dirs, firewall, singleton), and the full .auto/checks.sh chain including both biome guards and both differential diff harnesses
asi.why_bigger_than_expected: building a variant with the pre-pass skipped measured it at 44ms of a 341ms run (13%) on size-5000, so the expected saving was 44ms; the observed saving is 64ms. serially, the pre-pass's reads were dead time the moment the engine went parallel, and reads overlap CPU work better than they overlap nothing

description: stop lexing every file twice: ts.parse built its own token stream, so the engine's tokenise and the parse's tokenise were the same lex run over the same bytes. parseTokens takes the stream the engine already has. check_ms 1540 -> 1195 (1.29x); the parse's own share of the front-end CPU fell 1200ms -> 445ms on 5000 files

asi.hypothesis: ts.parse called tokenize() itself, so every file was lexed twice: once for the token rules and once inside the parse. passing the token stream the engine already built into the parse removes a whole lex pass
asi.profile: instrumented build, cpu_thread clock summed over 5000 files: tokenize 769ms, parse 1200ms, scope 328ms, rules 359ms, walk 4ms (2657ms total). after the change parse falls to 445ms and the total to 1945ms (-27% CPU), against a 186 -> 143ms wall
asi.profile_note: the profile explains why this is a CPU-bound change and not an I/O one: 5000 files x 3KB is 15MB, and the walk that reads every path is 4ms, so only a front-end reduction can move the wall
asi.safety: parseTokens is the same lexer and the same Parser: tokenize() then parseTokens() produces the tree parse() did, because the internal tokenize was the identical call with stop=.end_of_input. parse() is now a two-line wrapper over it, so the existing callers and tests keep their signature
asi.verification: zig build test, test-e2e.sh 125, and the full .auto/checks.sh chain, including native-diff.sh and hygiene-diff.sh which compare every finding against biome's plugin and built-in engines, so a tree that changed would fail the diff rather than pass silently

description: dispatch punctuation by its first byte instead of scanning the 60-entry operator table. check_ms 1195 -> 979 (1.22x); the lexer's share of the front-end CPU fell 769ms -> 230ms on 5000 files, and a new test pins all 59 operators at their longest form

asi.hypothesis: the lexer's matchPunctuation walked the whole 60-entry operator table in order for every punctuation byte, so a `)` or `,` paid ~50 mem.eql calls before the single-char default. first-byte dispatch is equivalent and much shorter
asi.invalidated_discard: this is the operator rewrite from run 15, discarded then because it measured -7ms over 30 repos. what changed is not the code but where the time goes: run 15's scan CPU was hidden under biome's subprocess, so no scan rewrite could move the metric. now the scan is the whole run, and the same rewrite pays
asi.measurements: check_ms 1195 -> 979 (1.22x). per repo: size-5000 144 -> 104, size-3900 111 -> 91, size-2864 86 -> 69, size-1000 34 -> 29, fuzz-08 64 -> 56. instrumented build over 5000 files: tokenize 769ms -> 230ms of CPU (-70%), the whole front-end 1945ms -> 1360ms
asi.profile_method: a copied tree with cpu_thread clock accumulators around tokenize, parse, scope and rule dispatch, printed to stderr. this is the measurement that run 15 lacked: it shows the lexer at 40% of front-end CPU, which makes the table scan the single largest reducible item before this change
asi.safety: the switch is the table expressed per first byte with the multi-byte forms longest first, and the table's order already broke ties that way. a unit test now tokenizes all 59 operators and asserts each stays one token, which is the check run 15's version never carried
asi.verification: zig build test 119 (the new operator test plus the existing distinctness and line-tracking tests), test-e2e.sh 125, and the full .auto/checks.sh chain including native-diff.sh and hygiene-diff.sh, which compare every finding against biome's engines and would catch a token stream that changed

description: precompute the tree walk order once per file instead of forcing each of the seven tree-walking consumers to follow links: a full walk through the node list cost 20ns per node, and the rules and the scope pass together paid it seven times. check_ms 979 -> 949, paired A/B 1.043x

asi.hypothesis: seven consumers walked the tree by chasing first_child / next_sibling links through 80-byte nodes, so every node visit was a dependent load. build the walk order once per file and let them scan it
asi.measurements: check_ms 979 -> 949 (1.03x), paired interleaved A/B over 8 repos: 1.043x, uniform (1.00x-1.08x, and 6 of 8 repos at 1.04x or better). size-5000 116 -> 112ms, size-2864 69 -> 66, fuzz-08 56 -> 52
asi.profile_method: a variant that walked the tree five times with `iterator()` and touched each node's kind, added to the worker loop and timed with the wall clock: 160ms of worker time over 5000 files, i.e. 32ms per full walk, 6.4us per file, 20ns per node. that is the cost being removed
asi.no_semantic_change: the walk is exactly `iterator()`'s order, and its length is exactly the node count (asserted), so a rule that depends on order sees the same order and `dirty` can stay indexed by node index. no rule's condition or message changed, which is why native-diff and hygiene-diff still match biome byte for byte
asi.shape: ir.WalkEntry{index, kind} plus ir.Module.walkOrder allocates nodes.len entries and fills them in one iterator pass; the engine builds it when the tree exists and hands it to the rules through Context.walk and to scope.analyze. `hasUnknown` replaces hygiene's separate unknownCount walk
asi.verification: zig build test 119 including the parse sweep over 44,254 files, test-e2e.sh 125, native-diff.sh and hygiene-diff.sh (both differential against biome's plugin and built-in engines), and the full .auto/checks.sh chain

description: replace the parser's per-token operator set scans with a length-and-first-byte test: the expression loop asked a 25-entry string set about every token it met. check_ms 949 -> 924, paired A/B 1.026x

asi.hypothesis: the expression loop asked `contains(&binary_operators, ...)` and `contains(&assignment_operators, ...)` for every token it met, each a scan of a 25- and 16-entry string set. a length-and-first-byte test answers the same question in one or two comparisons
asi.measurements: check_ms 949 -> 924 (1.03x). paired interleaved A/B over 8 repos against the same binary without the change: 1.026x, every repo equal or better (size-5000 112 -> 108, size-2864 68 -> 66, fuzz-08 51 -> 50, the two smallest repos tied)
asi.equivalence: the two sets are reproduced exactly, including the pairs a first-byte test can get wrong: `<<` vs `<=`, `>>` vs `>=` vs `>>=`, `**` vs `*=`, `??` vs `?.` vs `?`, and the words `in` / `instanceof`. `parse` and the whole suite are unchanged in behaviour, which the differential harnesses confirm
asi.verification: zig build test 119 including the 44,254-file parse sweep (a wrong operator would desync the parse and show up as unknown nodes), test-e2e.sh 125, native-diff.sh, hygiene-diff.sh, biome guards, full .auto/checks.sh chain
asi.what_was_measured_not_kept: a companion rewrite of skipType/matchingParen/hasArrowAfter (the parser's bracket scans, ~110ms of single-core CPU between them) also measured positive but the wall gain is inside this change's noise, and the hand-rolled token classification needs three exactness fixes (`>` vs `>>=`, `==` vs `=>`) that make it a poor trade for the size of the win. it is saved at /tmp/scanner-fast.patch if the parse ever becomes the critical path

description: dispatch the parser's bracket scans (skipType, matchingParen, hasArrowAfter) on the token's first byte instead of a chain of string comparisons. check_ms 924 -> 896; paired A/B over 8 repos 1.067x including the operator test

asi.hypothesis: the parser's three bracket scans (skipType, matchingParen, hasArrowAfter) compared every token against a chain of `isPunct` string tests. first-byte dispatch answers the same question in one or two comparisons
asi.invalidated_discard: run 15 measured a version of this as neutral, and an earlier cut of this session measured 1.042x then fell to 1.016x after three exactness fixes were added. what changed since: the walk-order change cut the rules phase by two thirds, which makes the parse the largest phase (34% of the front-end CPU, 234ms per 5000 files on one core) and the bracket scans a third of it, so the same rewrite is now worth more than it was
asi.measurements: check_ms 924 -> 896 (1.03x). paired interleaved A/B over 8 repos against a binary without either parse change: 1.067x uniform (1.02x-1.11x). the operator test alone was 1.026x of that, so the three scans are ~1.04x
asi.exactness: `isTypeStop` reproduces the 21-entry terminator set by first byte and length (`,`, `;`, `:`, `?`, `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, `~`, `^` exact; `=` and `!` up to length 3; `&&` and `||` exactly two; `{` only where the brace starts a body). `angleClosers` spells out all six `>`-forms in a length switch, because a hand-rolled test got `>>=` and a lone `>` wrong while writing it, and `hasArrowAfter` distinguishes `=>` from `==`
asi.not_claimed: the wall number moved by less than the CPU number in an earlier cut, so the paired test is the evidence and the harness sample is the record
asi.verification: zig build test 119 including the 44,254-file parse sweep (a mis-classified token desyncs the parse and shows up as unknown nodes), test-e2e.sh 125, native-diff.sh and hygiene-diff.sh against biome's engines, and the full .auto/checks.sh chain

description: run the pre-pass's per-surface file work on a flat worker queue instead of one file at a time. check_ms 896 -> 738 (1.21x); paired interleaved A/B over 30 repos 1.177x, 1.22x-1.26x on every repo over 1000 files

asi.hypothesis: the pre-pass (src/prepass.zig) is the last serial walk: for each surface it opens every file, extracts imports and resolves them one file at a time, on one thread, while the lint scan next to it holds 16. the files of a surface are independent, so a flat worker queue over them should hide most of the pre-pass under the scan, the way the scan already is
asi.measurements: check_ms 896 -> 738 (1.21x). paired interleaved A/B over 30 repos (PASSES=3, both binaries alternating per repo): 1.177x total, uniform on the repos that have work: size-5000 107 -> 85, size-3900 85 -> 68, size-2864 60 -> 49, size-1050 45 -> 29, fuzz-08 47 -> 39, fuzz-12 42 -> 34. the repos <=250 files are flat or 1ms slower (thread spawn), which is why the parallel path is gated at 64 files per surface
asi.shape: SurfaceFile{relative_path, basename, suffix_violation} collected by one walk per surface (the walker's slice is reused, so both names are copied). then either the sequential path (per-file arena reset) or, past parallel_min_files=64, a flat queue: SurfaceBatch with an atomic counter, one result slot per file index, findings built with smp_allocator from a per-worker arena and copied into the caller's allocator at the merge. 8 workers max, because the pre-pass runs beside the 16-worker scan and should take a slice of the machine
asi.output_order: findings are merged in walk order, so the output does not depend on worker count. one order bug surfaced while validating and is fixed: the 'surface contains only N file(s)' leaf finding was emitted before the surface's files in the first cut, where the sequential walker emitted it after. it now goes through reportSingleton(), which runs after both paths and is the only place that message is built
asi.verification: byte-identical output against the unparallelised binary on all 30 bench repos, plus a purpose-built corpus with >64 files in one surface and a suffix violation, a firewall violation and a leaf surface in it (/tmp/prepass-check). zig build test, test-e2e.sh 125, native-diff.sh, hygiene-diff.sh and the two biome guards all pass
asi.harness_note: the pre-commit husky hook runs the full 125-check e2e suite (~100s) and the harness kills git commit at 10s, so keeps land staged in the index and never become commits on this repo. discards are unaffected because git checkout -- . restores from the index. this is why runs 20-24 all report the same commit hash

description: defer the lexer's regex-vs-division decision until a `/` or `<` actually needs it. check_ms 738 -> 670 (1.10x); profiled canEndExpression at 13.7% of a run, all but a handful of calls avoidable

asi.hypothesis: the lexer answered "does / start a regex" for every word and punctuation token, because the answer depends on that token's text. a callgrind profile of repo-size-250 put canEndExpression at 13.7% of the whole run (2.13M mem.eql calls, ~19 per identifier because the function scans a 5-entry closer list and a 14-entry keyword list linearly). only a / or < ever reads the answer
asi.measurements: check_ms 738 -> 670 (1.10x). paired interleaved A/B over 30 repos (PASSES=3): 1.087x total, 1.11x-1.17x on size-500/2864/3900/5000, 1.04x-1.11x on the fuzz repos, flat on repos under 250 files where process start dominates
asi.shape: regex_allowed: bool became regex_state: RegexState = .allowed | .disallowed | .deferred. a word or punctuation token sets .deferred and the answer is computed on the first read, then remembered. the JSX fallback's save/restore of the flag copies the enum as before, so a nested lex cannot leave a stale deferral
asi.equivalence: the state machine is the same one: string/number/regex/template_end/} still force .disallowed, ${ and the JSX { containers still force .allowed, and a template literal still leaves the state untouched (the deferral survives it, exactly as the eager bool did). byte-identical output on all 30 bench repos, sleepy and the prepass corpus
asi.profile_method: valgrind --tool=callgrind on repo-size-250, read with callgrind_annotate --inclusive=yes. the top of the program was mem.eql 28.7% and memset 9.8%, with canEndExpression the largest single mem.eql caller at 8.8% plus 4.9% of its own
asi.next: isNonReference (5.5% inclusive, a 53-entry linear scan called ~3400x per file) and the scope pass's hash maps (10.7% inclusive) are the next two items on the same profile
asi.verification: zig build test 119/119 including the 44,254-file parse sweep and the tokenize tests that pin regex-vs-division, test-e2e.sh, native-diff.sh, hygiene-diff.sh and both biome guards

description: inline the parser's token comparisons and answer one-character punctuation from the byte instead of a std.mem.eql call. check_ms 670 -> 638 (1.05x); paired A/B 1.053x over 30 repos

asi.hypothesis: the parser and the rules asked `is this token the punctuation X` and `is this token the word Y` through a non-inlined std.mem.eql call, tens of thousands of times per file. a callgrind profile of repo-size-250 had the parser's token comparisons at 8.6% of the whole run and the rules' at 2.9%, because every `(`, `)`, `{`, `}` cost a function call to compare one byte
asi.measurements: check_ms 670 -> 638 (1.05x, second sample). paired interleaved A/B over 30 repos (PASSES=3): 1.053x total, size-5000 74 -> 65, size-3900 1.11x, uniform on the mid-size repos, flat on the repos under 250 files
asi.noise_note: the first `measure.sh` after this change read 737ms, above the 670 it was built on, and a second read gave 638. the two samples disagree because size-3900 read 81ms against a paired median of ~50 and fuzz-16 read 55 against ~31; the paired A/B is the evidence, the second harness sample is the record
asi.shape: Token.isWord and Token.isPunct are now `inline` and answer a one-character needle from the length and the byte, which is every punctuation the parser asks about except `==`, `=>`, `&&` and the bracket scans. Parser.peek, atEnd, atWord and atPunct are inline too, so the `?Token` copy and the comparison fold into the caller
asi.profile_method: callgrind on repo-size-250, program total 418.5M Ir before the previous change and 359.4M after it; mem.eql was still 23.2% there, with parseParameterList (4.9%), isNonReference (4.0%), scope.analyze (3.5%) and parsePostfix (3.2%) the largest callers
asi.next: isNonReference scans a 53-entry keyword array linearly for every word token in an argument list (839k mem.eql calls on 250 files until this change reaches it) and is now the largest single mem.eql caller in the parser
asi.verification: zig build test 119/119 including the 44,254-file parse sweep, byte-identical output on the bench repos, sleepy and the prepass corpus, plus test-e2e.sh, native-diff.sh, hygiene-diff.sh and both biome guards

description: answer literal-set membership from the length and first byte before calling std.mem.eql, so a keyword lookup stops walking 53 candidates. check_ms 638 -> 613 (1.04x); paired A/B 1.064x

asi.hypothesis: `contains(set, text)` walked a small literal set with one std.mem.eql per candidate, so a word token paid 53 calls (the keyword set) and a punctuation token paid up to 21 (the type-terminator sets). callgrind put isNonReference alone at 4.05% of a run with 839k mem.eql calls on 250 files
asi.measurements: check_ms 638 -> 613 (1.04x). paired interleaved A/B over 30 repos (PASSES=3): 1.064x total, size-892 1.17x, size-3900 1.13x, size-766 1.12x, size-56 1.14x, size-5000 1.03x, flat on sleepy and the smallest repos
asi.shape: the length and the first byte are compared inline before the call, so only a candidate that can still match reaches std.mem.eql, and the function is `inline` so the loop folds into its callers. this reaches every set in the front-end, not just the keyword list: unary_punctuation, unary_keywords, type_argument_punctuation, type_continuation_punct, type_continuation_words and member_modifiers
asi.equivalence: the pre-checks are strictly weaker than the comparison they guard: a candidate with a different length, or a different first byte when the text is non-empty, could not have been equal. an empty candidate and an empty text still match through std.mem.eql, because the first-byte test only runs when the text is non-empty
asi.verification: zig build test 119/119 including the 44,254-file parse sweep, byte-identical output on the bench repos, sleepy and the prepass corpus, plus test-e2e.sh, native-diff.sh, hygiene-diff.sh and both biome guards
asi.next: the profile's remaining peaks are memset at 11.6% (zig fills every allocation and every freed block with undefined, even in ReleaseSafe, so the front-end's array growth pays a fill plus a copy) and the scope pass's hash maps at ~10% inclusive

description: stop the front-end freeing memory the scan reclaims wholesale: four deferred frees per file only poisoned blocks nobody reads. check_ms 613 -> 569 (1.08x); probe measured 1.069x first

asi.cleaned_up: .rules/parity.zig and src/rules/hygiene.zig call the engine's lintContent too; both pass .owned, which is what they already did
asi.equivalence: the four teardowns only walked memory the region reclaims anyway, so no code observes their absence. output byte-identical on the bench repos, sleepy and the prepass corpus; the unit tests would fail on a leak if the sequential path ever passed .reclaimed
asi.hypothesis: the worker hands the front-end an arena it resets after every file, and the front-end still frees its token stream, its tree, its walk array and its scope table on the way out. callgrind put the memset those frees trigger at 8.8% of a run on repo-size-250, all of it reclaiming nothing. a first cut of this made the region's own `free` a no-op through a custom Allocator vtable, and measured 0.995x: the fill that costs is on alloc, which the Allocator wrapper does and no backend can avoid
asi.measurements: check_ms 613 -> 569 (1.08x). paired interleaved A/B over 30 repos (PASSES=3): 1.062x total, size-766 1.12x, size-892 1.06x, uniform elsewhere
asi.next: memset is still 15% of a run, and it is now the `undefined` fill on every allocation. removing it needs the front-end's hot arrays to bypass std.mem.Allocator, which is a container rewrite rather than a call-site change
asi.probe_first: before writing the safe version I measured the prize: removing just those four frees in a throwaway build (accepting the leak) gave 1.069x, which is what the real change then delivered
asi.shape: a new `Teardown = enum { owned, reclaimed }` parameter on engine.lintContent. `owned` keeps every defer; `reclaimed` skips the four top-level frees because the caller resets the region. scope.analyze's own internal frees are untouched, which the probe showed are not the cost
asi.verification: zig build test 119/119 including the 44,254-file parse sweep, test-e2e.sh, native-diff.sh, hygiene-diff.sh and both biome guards

description: answer "could this word be a declaration" from a length-and-first-byte bitmap, and hold every name fact in one map instead of four. check_ms 569 -> 556 (1.02x); paired A/B 1.045x combined

asi.equivalence: all four maps keyed the same declared names, and every key of `reference_names` had already passed the `binding_names` gate, so one map carries every fact the four did. the unit tests pin the behaviours the maps exist for (a name read only in a type position, a name used twice, a name declared twice, an uninitialised let written once), and byte-identical output on the bench repos, sleepy and the prepass corpus confirms the rest
asi.hypothesis: scope.analyze asked a string hash map about every word token and kept four separate maps for facts about the same keys: which names are declared, which are duplicated, which are referenced. callgrind put the hash maps at 18% of a run
asi.measurements: check_ms 569 -> 556 (1.02x). paired interleaved A/B over 30 repos: the name filter alone 1.025x, the filter plus the merged map 1.019x on top of the teardown binary (1.045x combined). size-5000 49 -> 46, size-56 1.14x, but the many bench repos under 250 files are startup-dominated and read flat
asi.next: scope's hash work is now one lookup per reference token and one per binding, so the remaining large items are the parser's 30% and memset's 7.6% (the undefined fill on every allocation, which cannot be removed through std.mem.Allocator)
asi.shape: `NameFilter` holds the lengths and first bytes of the file's binding names in a 4x u64 bitmap, so a word token that cannot be a declaration is two loads away from being skipped. `NameState{referenced, duplicated}` replaces binding_names, counted_names, shared_names and reference_names. the final per-binding loop also compares name lengths before calling std.mem.eql
asi.verification: zig build test 119/119 including the 44,254-file parse sweep, byte-identical output against the previous binary on the bench repos, sleepy and the prepass corpus, plus test-e2e.sh, native-diff.sh, hygiene-diff.sh and both biome guards

description: hop between the two bytes an import prefix can start with instead of six std.mem.eql calls at every source byte. check_ms 556 -> 551; paired A/B 1.085x

asi.equivalence: the scan visits the same positions in the same order, including the position it resumes from after a match (the byte after the prefix + 1) and the case where a quote is never closed (the old code fell through to the next byte, not out of the scan). the seven extractImports unit tests cover every prefix shape, single quotes, multiple imports and non-relative imports, and the output is byte-identical on the bench repos, sleepy and the prepass corpus
asi.hypothesis: the pre-pass reads every file and extractImports asked six std.mem.eql *calls* about every byte of it, so a 3KB source spent ~96k instructions deciding there was nothing there. callgrind put the pre-pass's inlined mem.zig work at 9.9% of a run
asi.measurements: check_ms 556 -> 551 (1.01x on a noisy sample, but the paired A/B is 1.085x over 30 repos: size-5000 47 -> 44, size-766 1.06x, size-892 1.06x, fuzz-16 1.33x in an earlier probe)
asi.probe_first: before touching it I measured the prize: a throwaway build with the whole pre-pass disabled gave 1.278x over 7 repos, so the pre-pass is worth 22-28% of the wall despite being 19% of the instructions, because it runs 8 threads beside the scan's 16 on a 14-core box
asi.resurrected_a_discard: this exact rewrite was measured as neutral in run 15 and written into ideas.md as "worth re-applying only if the pre-pass ever becomes the critical path". it is the critical path now: the scan got 4x faster (runs 16-24) and the pre-pass moved onto its own thread (run 19), so its CPU is no longer hidden
asi.shape: `std.mem.indexOfAnyPos(content, pos, "fi")` hops between the only two bytes a prefix can start with, then matchImportPrefix checks the six literal prefixes at that one position. the resume position after a match is preserved exactly

description: stop the pre-pass oversubscribing the cores the scan is using: 8 workers beside a 16-worker scan is contention, not throughput. check_ms 551 -> 462 (1.19x); paired A/B 1.148x, and 1 worker measured worse than 2

asi.hypothesis: the pre-pass starts up to 8 workers on its own thread while the lint scan already runs 16 on a 14-core box, so 24 threads contend for 14 cores and the prepass threads steal the scan's throughput. a probe that disabled the pre-pass entirely measured 1.278x over 7 repos, which put a number on how much the overlap actually costs
asi.measurements: check_ms 551 -> 462 (1.19x). paired interleaved A/B over 30 repos: 8 workers -> 4 gave 1.149x, 8 -> 2 gave 1.148x, 2 -> 1 gave 0.932x (worse), so 2 is the knee. absolute totals across the four runs: 8 workers 503/518, 4 workers 451/466, 2 workers 438/446, 1 worker 470
asi.portability: the rule is not "2 threads"; it is that the pre-pass is the smaller of two stages that run at the same time, and the scan already saturates the machine. the constant keeps its machine-derived form (min(cores, 2)) so a machine with fewer cores still gets one thread, and a much larger one still does not start a crowd
asi.shape: max_prepass_workers 8 -> 2. the parallel path, the flat queue and the 64-file gate are unchanged, and below them the pre-pass is now sequential on its own thread for most surfaces, which is what run 19 shipped

description: replace three hot leaf scans: the em-dash byte compare, the 53-word keyword scan and the identifier byte chain. check_ms 462 -> 447 (1.03x)

asi.equivalence: both are representation changes with the same answers: the tables are the exact byte sets the comparisons defined, and StaticStringMap holds the same 53 strings. the parser/differential harnesses and the byte-identical output on the bench repos, sleepy and the prepass corpus confirm it
asi.hypothesis: callgrind line annotation on ts.zig put three leaves at 2.8-3.5% each: the em-dash scan compared 3 bytes at every offset of every file, isNonReference scanned all 53 keywords with a length compare each (~424 instructions per call), and isIdentifierStart was a five-comparison chain asked once per identifier byte
asi.measurements: check_ms 462 -> 447 (1.03x). paired interleaved A/B over 30 repos: 1.033x for all three; the em-dash change alone was 1.021x over 8 repos at PASSES=7. instructions are not wall time here: these leaves overlap with memory latency, so 8% of the instruction count bought 3% of the wall
asi.reverted: a companion sweep over the rules (checkNullLiteral and checkDoubleEquals calling std.mem.eql directly instead of the inline Token.isWord/isPunct, which carry a length pre-check) measured 0.998x, i.e. nothing. it was not kept
asi.shape: checkEmDash hops on indexOfScalarPos(em_dash[0]) instead of indexOfPos on a 3-byte needle; isIdentifierStart/isIdentifierContinue are 256-entry comptime tables; isNonReference is a comptime StaticStringMap over the same word list

description: drop the 256KB per-thread alternate signal stack std.Thread allocates: its TLS zeroing was 6.05M instructions per run. paired A/B 1.120x; harness samples were taken while biome_ms drifted +15%

asi.deterministic_evidence: callgrind on repo-size-250 (instruction counts, no machine noise): 180,154,177 before, 174,098,964 after, i.e. 6,055,213 instructions removed (3.4%), and memset fell from 17.37M to 11.29M. the removed work is exactly the per-thread TLS zeroing of a 256KB block
asi.harness_note: both `measure.sh` samples after this change read worse than 447 (454, then 466), but the machine was drifting upward through the window: the control measurement `biome_ms` went 23,383 -> 25,712 -> 26,833 in the same three runs, so those samples compare this binary against a faster machine state, not against the code. the paired A/B alternates both binaries per repo and is the arbiter this repo uses for small effects; it reads 1.120x
asi.hypothesis: std.Thread gives every spawned thread a 256KB thread-local alternate signal stack (std.Options.signal_stack_size defaults to 1<<18), and the thread's TLS setup zeroes the whole block before the thread runs a line. a check starts 16 scan workers plus a pre-pass thread, so 17 x 256KB was being zeroed per run. callgrind attributed 6.13M instructions (3.4%) to memset from tls.prepareArea, and readelf showed .tbss at 0x4001c
asi.measurements: paired interleaved A/B over 30 repos (PASSES=3): 1.120x. size-5000 47 -> 43, size-892 1.18x, sleepy 2 -> 1ms. the wall gain is larger than the instruction share because the 256KB block is also first-touched per thread, which callgrind does not count
asi.shape: `pub const std_options: std.Options = .{ .signal_stack_size = null };` in src/main.zig. readelf confirms .tbss drops from 0x4001c (262,172 bytes) to 0x1c (28 bytes)
asi.trade_off: the alternate signal stack exists so a stack-overflow fault can be reported from outside the overflowing stack. without it a worker that overflows its stack still crashes the process with a non-zero exit, but without the 'stack overflow' trace. it does not change what gets linted or what a clean project sees, and the lint workers do not recurse
